output.title: Why paints make brown, but light makes white
output.summary: Paints mix by subtracting light, so many pigments together absorb more colors and often look brown or muddy. Light mixes by adding light, so red, green, and blue light together can make white.
learningObjectives: Tell the difference between mixing pigments and mixing light.
Explain why mixing many paints usually makes a darker, browner color.
Explain why mixing colored lights can make white.
Use the words additive and subtractive in a simple way.
misconceptionNotes: Mixing all colors always does not make the same result. Paints and light behave differently because paints absorb some light, while lights add more light to the eye.

sections.text: Your paint palette shows pigments on a surface. When you mix them, the new color usually gets darker and duller because each paint takes away some of the light. When you mix colored lights, the light gets brighter and can become white if enough colors are added together.

Paints make brown because pigments absorb parts of the light, so mixing many paints removes more and more colors from the light reaching your eyes. Light makes white because colored lights add together, and enough different light can combine into white.

Your eyes only see the light that bounces off an object or comes from a screen or lamp. Paint works by subtracting light: each pigment absorbs some colors and reflects the rest. Light works by adding light: when red, green, and blue lights shine together, your eyes receive more total light and can see white.

Paint pigments are tiny particles. Different pigments absorb different parts of white light, so mixing several pigments usually leaves fewer colors to reflect, which often looks brown, gray, or black. Colored lights are beams of light; when beams overlap, the eye adds them together. Red plus green light can look yellow, and red, green, and blue together can look white.

Try this at home or in class: shine a red flashlight and a green flashlight on the same white wall. The overlapping spot should look yellowish, not brown. Now think about mixing finger paints: if you blend many different paints, the result usually gets muddy because each pigment absorbs more light.

Scientists learned that color depends on both light and materials over many years. In the 1800s, James Clerk Maxwell studied color mixing with light and showed that different colored lights can combine to match other colors, including white.
Which one is additive: mixing paint or mixing light? Why? If you are unsure, remember this clue: paint on paper takes away light, but a lamp or screen sends out light.
If you want, you can learn about complementary colors, why printers use cyan, magenta, yellow, and black, and why screens use red, green, and blue.

output.title: Why a Bigger Drum Sounds Deeper
output.summary: A bigger drum usually sounds deeper because its drumhead vibrates more slowly, which makes a lower pitch. The size is only part of the story—how tight the drumhead is also matters.
learningObjectives: Explain that a drum makes sound when its head vibrates.

misconceptionNotes: A bigger drum is not automatically louder; bigger drums usually sound deeper because of lower pitch, not because the sound is stronger.

sections.text: When you hit a drum, the top skin shakes back and forth. Your ears hear that shaking as sound.
A bigger drum sounds deeper because its drumhead usually vibrates more slowly, which makes a lower pitch. The drumhead’s tightness also changes the pitch.

Sound from a drum comes from vibration. A slower vibration makes a lower pitch, and a faster vibration makes a higher pitch. On a bigger drum, the drumhead has more space to move, so it tends to vibrate more slowly than a smaller drumhead.

The drumhead is the part that mainly makes the sound. The shell underneath helps the sound spread and ring out. If the drumhead is tighter, it usually makes a higher pitch; if it is looser, it usually makes a lower pitch.

Try this: make a rubber band “drum” over a bowl or container. Stretch the band tighter and pluck it again. It should sound higher when tighter and lower when looser. That is the same idea as a real drumhead.
Drums are very old instruments and have been used by many cultures for thousands of years. People have long changed drum size and tightness to get different sounds.
Which drum should sound deeper: a small drum or a big drum? What else can change the pitch besides size?
If you want to explore more, listen to different drums: snare drum, tom-tom, bass drum, and hand drum. Compare how size and tightness change the pitch you hear.

output.title: Why clay goes hard and changes colour in a kiln
output.summary: Clay becomes hard in a kiln because heat drives off remaining water and causes the tiny particles to bond together. Its colour can change because minerals in the clay, especially iron-bearing ones, react differently at high temperatures and in different kiln atmospheres.
learningObjectives: Explain why unfired clay is soft and brittle.
Describe how heat makes clay particles bond together.
Explain why kiln temperature and oxygen conditions can change clay colour.
misconceptionNotes: Clay does not just 'dry out' in the kiln. Drying removes liquid water, but firing also causes lasting chemical and structural changes that make the pot hard.
A colour change is not just paint burning off; it often comes from changes in the clay’s own minerals during firing.

sections.text: When a clay pot goes into a kiln, it comes out much harder, stronger, and often a different colour. The change happens because the clay is being heated far beyond ordinary drying.

Heat removes the last water from the clay and then makes its tiny particles fuse and partially melt together, which hardens the pot. The colour changes because the minerals in the clay react differently at kiln temperatures, and the amount of oxygen in the kiln can also affect the final colour.

Raw clay is made of very small plate-like minerals plus water. Before firing, that water lets the particles slide past one another, which is why wet clay is easy to shape. As the kiln heats up, chemically bound water is driven off and the particles begin to bond more strongly; at higher temperatures, some material can soften enough to help particles stick together, making the clay body dense and rigid.

A kiln works by raising the temperature of the clay in a controlled way. In the first stage, remaining water leaves the clay. Later, the clay minerals change structure, and the body begins to sinter: grain contacts grow and pores shrink. If the clay contains fluxes, parts of it can form a glassy phase that helps lock the shape in place. Color changes happen because minerals such as iron can oxidize or reduce depending on how much oxygen reaches the pot.

Try this thought experiment: if you heated the same clay sample in more oxygen, and then in less oxygen, would you expect the same colour? Usually not, because the kiln atmosphere changes the chemistry of iron-bearing minerals. That is why two pots made from the same clay can fire to different colours if the firing conditions are different.

People have been firing clay for thousands of years; pottery is among the oldest human technologies. Early potters discovered that heat could turn soft clay into durable vessels, long before anyone understood the chemistry behind the process.

1) Is fired clay hard because it is only dry? No — firing changes the clay itself. 2) Can the same clay fire to different colours? Yes — temperature, minerals, and kiln atmosphere all matter. 3) Does every clay become the same colour in the kiln? No — clay composition and firing conditions can produce many outcomes.

If you want to go deeper, look up the terms 'sintering,' 'vitrification,' and 'kiln atmosphere.' These explain how a porous clay body becomes a ceramic material with new strength, texture, and colour.

Different firing conditions can make the same clay body come out different colours.
People have fired clay into pottery for thousands of years.
Pottery is one of the oldest human technologies.

output.title: Abstract painting: what is it a picture of?
output.summary: Abstract paintings may not be pictures of a specific object or scene. They use color, shape, line, and form to make an effect, and viewers often interpret them in different ways.
learningObjectives: Explain why an abstract painting may not have a single recognizable subject.
Describe how abstract painters use visual elements like color and shape.

misconceptionNotes: It is a common mistake to assume every painting must show a recognizable object, person, or place. Abstract painting can be non-representational, so its subject may be emotion, composition, movement, or visual rhythm rather than a literal scene.

sections.text: You are probably seeing an abstract painting. That means the artist may not be trying to show a real-world object, person, or place in a literal way.
It may not be a picture of any one thing. Abstract paintings often do not represent a recognizable subject, and instead use color, shape, line, and form to create meaning or feeling.

A picture can either represent something specific or work without a clear subject. In abstract art, the artist may focus on the arrangement of visual elements rather than on copying what something looks like in real life.

Look for clues in the painting itself: repeated shapes, strong contrasts, color patterns, direction of brushstrokes, and balance across the canvas. These parts can guide your interpretation even when there is no obvious object to name.
Try this: describe the painting without naming objects. Say what colors, shapes, textures, and movements you notice. Then ask yourself what mood or energy those choices create.

Abstract art became an important movement in the early 20th century, and artists such as Wassily Kandinsky are often linked with its development. Museums and reference works describe abstract art as a major shift away from direct representation.

If you cannot identify a clear object, that does not mean the painting has no meaning. The meaning may come from the visual experience itself, or from the artist’s use of abstraction rather than from a literal subject.

If you want to go deeper, compare this painting with a realistic portrait or landscape. Notice how the realistic work points to a named subject, while the abstract work may ask you to respond to color, structure, and feeling instead.
